attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, stated in the first person.

semantics.note: Firm statement of belief that no more than 1M Blackwell GPUs are in service. The drafter's wording adds 'about' (a tolerance) and 'out of roughly three million shipped', which this sentence does not assert. The contract correctly drops the tolerance.

contract.note: An upper bound of 1M operational packages over May 1–12, 2026 is an ordinary, fair plain reading. Excluding hardware still being installed matches 'actually in service'.

evidence.note: Modelled estimate of about 1.9M operational packages, dated end-2025. It is a model with installation assumptions, not a verified May 2026 count, and it covers a different period. Context only, though it points against the claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no verified May 2026 count of in-service Blackwell GPUs. The one contrary item is a modelled end-2025 estimate, which does not meet the contract's requirement for a reliable estimate or deduplicated count for the target period. Nothing establishes the upper bound either. The evidence available does not settle it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own first-person prediction in his newsletter.

semantics.note: 'I also think ... will eventually' is a firm 'will' forecast with no deadline. Reading 'similar problems' as the compute capacity limits described in the preceding Anthropic sentence fits the context. Slow construction is kept as the predicted cause.

contract.note: The open horizon, early resolution only on a documented constraint caused by construction delays, and no failure from mere absence over a finite period are all fair to the words.

evidence.note: CNBC, Sept 2026: OpenAI is exploring smaller 20–30 MW deals for faster capacity. Consistent with compute pressure, but it names no OpenAI service constraint caused by construction delays.

reviews.rationale: This is an open-ended 'eventually' forecast. The packet shows no documented OpenAI capacity constraint caused by slow construction, so the early-resolution rule is not met, and the absence of such an event so far is not failure. The outcome stays open.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The revision keeps his 'suggesting' framing and the 'if that's true' conditional on the NVIDIA inference, and keeps his word 'digested'.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to invent thresholds for 'very, very few', 'years worth' and 'digested'. Any score would depend on definitions the speaker never supplied.

evidence.note: CBRE reports record 2025 net absorption in North American primary markets. Regional capacity data for a different period; it cannot settle an undefined global completion claim or NVIDIA inventory.

reviews.rationale: This is a tentative suggestion plus a conditional inference, and its key terms ('very, very few', 'years worth', 'digested') have no measure, population or rate. Scoring it would mean supplying definitions the speaker did not give, so it is not adjudicable.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'probably' and the no-schedule clause. The statement is hedged with 'probably', which policy treats as probabilistic and does not score.

contract.note: The contract turns hedged 'probably' into a scored majority-by-count threshold, applies a plain reading to hedged language (which policy forbids), and picks the population and the Q1 2026 window itself.

evidence.note: Sightline, Feb 2026: about 11GW of 2026 capacity has no visible construction. Weighted by capacity, not project count, and it does not assess remaining schedules. Context only.

reviews.rationale: 'It's probably barely under construction' is probabilistic, rhetorical framing ('Pick a data center'). Under policy, hedged language is not scored. The contract's majority threshold and choice of population are evaluator inventions, so the claim is not adjudicable.
